title: RRIF Basics
summary: CONVERT BY 71 → WITHDRAW MINIMUM → PLAN THE TAX
subtitle: An RRSP is for building up. A RRIF is for drawing down. At 71, that switch happens whether you’re ready or not.

blocks.text: An RRSP is for building up. A RRIF is for drawing down.
They hold the same kinds of investments, and both shelter growth from tax. The difference is direction: you put money into an RRSP, and you must take money out of a RRIF.
At the end of the year you turn 71, that switch happens whether you’re ready or not. Knowing how it works in advance is what makes the move smooth instead of costly.
Keep more of your retirement savings by planning the switch before it’s forced on you.
blocks.detail: A few choices made years before 71 can lower your lifetime tax and protect your Old Age Security.
blocks.extra: Section 05 covers three choices to make before you convert.

blocks.text: By December 31 of the year you turn 71, your RRSP has to become something else. You have three options.

items.title: Convert it to a RRIF. This is what most Canadians do. You keep your investments and the tax shelter, and start taking yearly withdrawals.
Buy an annuity. You get guaranteed income for life, but you give up flexibility and control.
Take it all out in cash. This is almost never the right choice. The whole balance becomes taxable income in one year, usually at the highest rate you’ll ever pay.

blocks.text: Miss the deadline, and the RRSP can be closed and the whole balance taxed that year. Some providers move it into a RRIF for you, but don’t count on it. That’s the outcome to plan around.

items.title: “A RRIF is a completely different investment than my RRSP.”
items.text: It holds the same things under new rules. Your stocks, funds and GICs can move straight over. What changes is that deposits stop and yearly minimum withdrawals begin.

sections.title: The mandatory minimum, and how it grows

blocks.text: Every year, you must take out at least a set percentage of what your RRIF was worth on January 1.
The percentage is set by federal rules and rises with your age. At 71 it’s 5.28%. At 75, 5.82%. At 80, 6.82%. At 95 and over, it’s 20%.
There’s no maximum, so you can always take out more than the minimum. And in the calendar year you open the RRIF, there’s no required withdrawal at all.

items.title: Age 95 and over

blocks.text: Every dollar you take out is taxed as regular income in the year you take it. That’s the key thing to plan around, and it’s what the rest of this lesson is about. Your provider holds back tax only on amounts above the minimum, so you may owe more at tax time.

sections.title: Why mandatory withdrawals can cost you twice

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: WHY MANDATORY WITHDRAWALS CAN COST YOU TWICE

RRIF withdrawals count as income, and that matters beyond the tax bill. Old Age Security starts getting clawed back once your net income passes a threshold: $95,323 for 2026. You repay 15% of every dollar above that line. Large RRIF withdrawals, stacked on CPP and any pension, can push a retiree over it. The frustrating part is that the withdrawal wasn’t optional. The minimum is required, and the percentage climbs every year whether or not you need the money. That’s why many Canadians plan their drawdown well before 71, taking money out of an RRSP in lower-income early retirement years, when the tax cost is smaller, to shrink the balance that will later force bigger withdrawals.

sections.title: Three things worth knowing before you convert

blocks.text: You can use a younger spouse’s age. If your spouse or partner is younger, you can base your minimum withdrawals on their age instead of yours. That means a lower percentage, a smaller required withdrawal and more money left growing. You choose this when you set up the RRIF, before the first payment, so raise it before you convert.

Converting at 65 opens two doors. You don’t have to wait until 71. RRIF payments you receive at 65 or older count as pension income. They can qualify for the pension income credit, on up to $2,000 a year, and can be split with a spouse on your tax returns. Both can lower a household’s total tax.

Taking out more than the minimum is sometimes smart. In a low-income year, taking out more than required and moving the extra into a TFSA can smooth your lifetime tax bill. Money in a TFSA grows tax-free and, unlike a RRIF withdrawal, doesn’t count as income later.

items.title: “I should always withdraw the bare minimum to keep taxes low.”
items.text: Not always. Taking the minimum leaves a bigger balance behind, which forces bigger withdrawals later. Whatever is left at death is generally taxed heavily unless it goes to a spouse. Sometimes taking more in a low-income year costs less over a lifetime than taking the minimum every year.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: WHAT HAPPENS TO A RRIF WHEN YOU DIE

There’s a fourth thing to know, and it rarely comes up until it’s urgent. With no planning, the full value of a RRIF is generally added to your income on your final tax return in the year you die. It’s often the largest tax bill your estate will ever face. There’s a fix, and it mirrors the TFSA successor holder from the TFSA Basics lesson. Name a spouse or common-law partner as successor annuitant, not just a beneficiary, and the RRIF continues in their name. No tax is triggered, and nothing closes. If you leave it to a financially dependent child or grandchild with a disability instead, the money can often move into their RDSP rather than becoming one big taxable lump sum. Check the form on file with your RRIF provider. A beneficiary and a successor annuitant sound alike but are treated differently.

items.title: I know my RRSP must be converted by December 31 of the year I turn 71.
I understand every RRIF withdrawal is fully taxable as income.
I’ve considered whether converting earlier, at 65, would help with pension splitting or the pension income credit.
If my spouse is younger, I know I can base my minimum withdrawals on their age, but only if I choose it at setup.
I’ve thought about whether large mandatory withdrawals later could push me into OAS clawback territory.

blocks.text: Bernard’s early start
paragraphs: Bernard retired from his job as a high school shop teacher in Sudbury at sixty-three. He had a healthy RRSP, a teacher’s pension and no need to touch his savings. His plan was simple: leave the RRSP alone and let it grow until the rules forced him to act at seventy-one.

His daughter, an accountant, asked to see the numbers over Thanksgiving dinner. Between sixty-three and seventy, she pointed out, his income would be at its lowest: no salary, CPP and OAS not started yet. Those were the cheapest years he would ever have to take money out of an RRSP.

Bernard frowned. Paying tax on money he didn’t need felt backward. But she kept going. If he waited, his RRSP would be much larger at seventy-one. The required withdrawals would stack on top of his pension, CPP and OAS, and could push him past the OAS clawback line in his late seventies.

He slept on it. The next week, Bernard made his choice. Starting at sixty-four, he would take out a modest amount each year, pay tax at a low rate and move whatever he didn’t spend into his TFSA. He also named his wife, Claudette, as successor annuitant when he set up the RRIF.

The twist came later. At seventy-two, Bernard’s required withdrawal was small enough that his income stayed below the clawback line. His full OAS cheque arrived every month. Meanwhile, his TFSA had quietly grown into a tax-free fund he could tap for anything.
That Thanksgiving, he handed his daughter the turkey carving knife. “You earned it,” he said. “You carved seven years off my tax problem.”

blocks.text: Your RRSP must become a RRIF, an annuity or cash by December 31 of the year you turn 71, and cashing out is almost never right. RRIF withdrawals are required, rise as a percentage with age and are taxed as income. Because they can push you into OAS clawback territory, many Canadians benefit from drawing down an RRSP in lower-income years, well before 71.
A few low-tax years before 71 can protect your income for decades after.
blocks.detail: Planning your withdrawals early keeps more of your savings, your pension and your Old Age Security.
blocks.extra: Section 08 helps you map your own conversion plan.

items.title: If you’re within ten years of 71, estimate your RRSP balance at conversion and the minimum withdrawal on that amount.
If you’re retired but not yet 71, ask whether these are low-income years worth using to draw down early.
If you have a younger spouse or partner, raise the younger-spouse option with your adviser before you convert, not after.

blocks.text: Worksheet: your conversion plan

items.title: RRIF
items.text: Registered Retirement Income Fund. The account an RRSP turns into, with required yearly withdrawals.

items.title: Minimum withdrawal
items.text: The share of your January 1 balance you must take out each year. It rises with age.

items.title: OAS clawback
items.text: The 15% recovery tax on Old Age Security once net income passes a threshold.

items.title: Younger-spouse election
items.text: Basing your minimum withdrawals on a younger spouse’s age, which lowers the amount required.

items.title: Pension income splitting
items.text: Sharing eligible pension income with a spouse on your tax returns to lower your household’s total tax.
